I teach in a school for kids with social, emotional and behavioural problems and when I first started around 6 years ago I made up a story on the spur of the moment to get them writing. There is a mental health unit across the road from the school that has a residential wing which is generally used by people with eating disorders but our pupils don't know that. All they really know about the place is that they go there to get diagnosed with ADHD.

Anyway, one day I told them that the unit was once home to a patient who had been caught dressing up as a clown to sneak around circuses and fairgrounds to abduct and eat children. He found a way to tunnel from the grounds of the unit into the boiler room of the school and still picks one off every 25 years (handily enough, the last time magically always happens to be almost 25 years to the day although it sometimes takes them a while to figure this out).

The best thing about the Clown in the Boiler Room story is that it has taken on a life of its own and gets handed down each year with very little input from me.

When I was about 7 or 8, the neighbors across the street from me were the ones that I spent most of my time with, 2 boys about my age and a younger girl. Their dad was a truck driver and would drink pretty often, so he would tell us the craziest stories from when he was on the road. I'd take them with a grain of salt. But one that really stuck was the one of a lady on the highway that would block the roads.

He said that driving down in the middle of the night, he was talking to his copilot when a car was driving on the other side of the road honking and switching lights at them, but they would usually just slow down and be careful ahead. They kept driving and saw more cars doing the same. That was curious, but kept going. About a mile down the road, they saw this figure of a lady walking in the middle of the road. She was wearing a white dress and couldn't see her face. The guy stepped on the brakes long before they would get any closer, he honked at her and she started walking towards them. He didn't say nothing about the way she walked, but it was pretty scary. They had to back out of there until they were able to make a U-turn and drove about 5 hours just to avoid that road.

I still remember clearly how he told us about it. He was soaked in sweat and wasn't drinking, which was one of the first thing he'd do as soon as he would get home. He was shaking and while he was talking, I felt chills on my back. They moved out of there a couple of years after that. We never talked about it again.
